title: Amendment 3: Pledge of Allegiance and Student-Led Prayer in Public Schools

context.text: Referred to the ballot by the Alabama Legislature as House Bill 511 (Act 2026-379), sponsored by Rep. Reed Ingram (R-Pike Road). Alabama has no citizen initiative; the Legislature refers amendments to voters under Sections 284 and 285 of the Constitution of Alabama of 2022, and a majority of those voting on the question approves. The House passed it on March 10, 2026 (94-4, per the Alabama Reflector) and the Senate on April 8, 2026 (30-0).

question.text: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of Alabama of 2022, to require local boards of education to adopt policies requiring each public K-12 school to recite The Pledge of Allegiance to the United States flag at the beginning of each school day; and to require local boards of education to adopt a policy authorizing student-initiated and student-led prayer. Proposed by Act 2026-379.

summary.text: The amendment would require each local board of education to adopt policies requiring every public K-12 school, at the start of each school day, to conduct the Pledge of Allegiance and give students the opportunity to voluntarily recite it, and to allow a prayer that is initiated and led by a student, with no student required to participate. Policies must ensure students may opt out of the Pledge or the prayer based on their own beliefs, and violations may be reported to the local superintendent, who must review them. The Fair Ballot Commission's statement notes the Constitution currently contains no such requirement, and states: "There are no costs or taxes associated with Amendment 3."

measure.yesMeans: Adds to the Alabama Constitution a requirement that local boards adopt policies for a daily Pledge of Allegiance in every public K-12 school and for student-initiated, student-led prayer, with an opt-out for students.
measure.noMeans: The Alabama Constitution is not changed: it continues to contain no requirement that local boards adopt policies for a daily Pledge of Allegiance or for student-initiated, student-led prayer.

argumentsFor.text: Rep. Reed Ingram (R-Pike Road), the sponsor, said: "A lot of these kids want to be exposed to God or have that opportunity to worship, and this gives them that. They don't have that opportunity at home because their parents may work two or three jobs and work on Sunday."

argumentsAgainst.text: Rev. Julie Conrady of the Unitarian Universalist Church of Birmingham and Tuscaloosa, speaking about the prayer legislation, said: "Imposing these bills would create a further hardship to our students of diverse religious beliefs in our state, and so it is essential that we protect their beliefs and their parents' choice in making those decisions about which faith communities they are a part of and which doctrines they are exposed to." WSFA also reported that opponents argue the legislation conflicts with the First Amendment and the principle of separation of church and state.

researchNotes: The Alabama Secretary of State's page of Fair Ballot Commission ballot statements (sos.alabama.gov/alabama-votes/voter/ballot-measures/statewide) lists exactly four statewide amendments for the Nov. 3, 2026 general election, numbered 1-4 in this order; the question text is the description in the enrolled Act, confirmed against the Commission's ballot statement (which adds "Proposed by Act 2026-xxx"). Alabama issues no voter pamphlet and no registered ballot-measure committees were found. The arguments are from news coverage of committee hearings on the bill (HB 511 and a companion), not from a campaign. House vote reported as 94-4 by the Alabama Reflector; other outlets reported 94-3, so the House count is attributed to the Reflector.
